'''''Acacia cyclops''''', commonly known as '''coastal wattle''',<ref name=FB>{{FloraBase | name = Acacia cyclops | id = 3282}}</ref> '''cyclops wattle''', '''one-eyed wattle''', '''red-eyed wattle''', '''redwreath acacia''', '''western coastal wattle''', and as '''rooikrans''' or '''rooikrans acacia''' in South Africa,<ref name=lucid>{{cite web|url= https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/acacia_cyclops.htm|title=''Acacia cyclops''|access-date=2 February 2019|work= Special edition of Environmental Weeds of Australia for Biosecurity Queensland|year=2016|publisher=Identic Pty Ltd}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]]. The [[Noongar]] peoples of Western Australia know the plant as '''wilyawa''' or '''woolya wah'''.<ref name=mooro>{{cite web|url=https://www.joondalup.wa.gov.au//Files/Plants%20and%20People%20in%20Mooro%20Country.pdf|title=Plants and People in Mooro Country: Nyungar Plant Use in Yellagonga Regional Park|year=2011|access-date=10 May 2020|publisher=[[City of Joondalup]]|archive-date=8 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200308170737/https://www.joondalup.wa.gov.au//Files/Plants%20and%20People%20in%20Mooro%20Country.pdf}}</ref> It is a dense shrub or tree with narrowly oblong to elliptic [[phyllode]]s, spherical heads of golden yellow flowers, and linear, leathery [[Pod (fruit)|pods]] with colourful seeds. The species is native to Australia, and is distributed along the west coast of [[Western Australia]] as far north as [[Leeman, Western Australia|Leeman]], and along the south coast into [[South Australia]]. It has been introduced to several other countries.

==Description==
''Acacia cyclops'' is a shrub or small tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|1–6|m}} and has [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] branchlets. Its phyllodes are ascending, narrowly oblong to elliptic or egg-shaped with the narrower end toward the base, mostly {{cvt|40–95|mm}} long and {{cvt|6–15|mm}} wide, leathery and glabrous with three or four main veins. The flowers are borne in two spherical heads in axils on [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] {{cvt|4–12|mm}} long, each head {{cvt|5–7|mm}} in diameter often with 60 to 75 golden yellow flowers. Flowering occurs from September to May, and the pods are linear, up to {{cvt|150|mm}} long and {{cvt|7–16|mm}} wide, thickly leathery and glabrous. The seeds are elliptic, {{cvt|5–7|mm}} long, glossy dark brown to black, with an orange to scarlet attachment encircling the seed.<ref name="FB" /><ref name="lucid" /><ref name="foa">{{cite web |last1=Cowan |first1=Richard S. |last2=Maslin |first2=Bruce R. |last3=Kodela |first3=Phillip G. |title='' Acacia cyclops'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Acacia%20cyclops |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water: Canberra. |access-date=19 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |title=''Acacia cyclops'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/wattle/text/entities/acacia_cyclops.htm |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study |access-date=19 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="www">{{cite web |title=''Acacia cyclops'' |url=https://worldwidewattle.com/speciesgallery/cyclops.php |publisher=World Wide Wattle |access-date=19 August 2025}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Acacia cyclops'' was first formally described by the botanist [[George Don]] in 1832 in his book ''A General History of Dichlamydeous Plants''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Acacia cyclops'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/466560 |publisher=APNI|access-date=18 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="Don">{{cite book |last1=Don |first1=George |title=A General History of Dichlamydeous Plants |volume=2 |date=1832 |location=London |page=404 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/62428#page/418/mode/1up |access-date=18 August 2025}}</ref> The [[botanical name|specific epithet]] (''cyclops'') may be an allusion to [[Cyclops]] in [[Homer]]'s [[Odyssey]] of [[Odysseus]] who gouged out the eye of [[Polyphemus]] with a burnt stake, because the seeds are black with a bright red attachment to the [[ovule]].<ref name="George">{{cite book |last1=George |first1=Alex S. |last2=Sharr |first2=Francis A. |title=Western Australian Plant Names and Their Meanings - A Glossary |date=2023 |publisher=Four Gables Press |location=Kardinya |isbn=978-0-6456295-3-8 |page=179 |edition=fifth}}</ref>

This wattle may be related to ''[[Acacia redolens]]'' and is quite similar to ''[[Acacia veronica]]''. It is about as drought tolerant as ''[[Acacia saligna]]'' but is also able to tolerate sea spray.<ref name=foa/>

==Distribution and habitat==
Coastal wattle is widespread and apparently discontinuous in coastal and near-coastal areas mainly between [[Denmark, Western Australia|Denmark]] and [[Israelite Bay, Western Australia|Israelite Bay]] and from [[Leeman, Western Australia|Leemann]] to [[Yorketown, South Australia|Yorketown]] and the [[Yorke Peninsula]] in [[South Australia]].<ref name="foa" /><ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="www" /> It grows in coastal heath or scrubland on coastal sand dunes and on limestone.<ref name="foa" /><ref name="FB" />

''Acacia cyclops'' has invaded similar habitats in other areas within Australia, mostly semi-arid  regions of inland south-eastern South Australia where it is considered a problem. It is also found in parts of South Africa along roadsides and waterways as well as in parts of California in wetland habitats and among [[riparian]] communities.<ref name=lucid/> It has been introduced to the [[Azores]], California, the [[Canary Islands]], the [[Cape Provinces]], [[Cyprus]], [[Ethiopia]], [[Morocco]], [[Namibia]], [[Northern Provinces]], [[Palestine]], Portugal, [[Sicily]], Spain and [[Saint Helena]].<ref name="PoW)">{{cite web |title=''Acacia cyclops'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:470108-1 |publisher=Plants of the World Online |access-date=19 August 2025}}</ref>

In South Africa it is considered to be one of the most widespread alien invasive species, though the roots are susceptible to attack by various species of ''[[Ganoderma]]'' fungi.<ref name="Tchotet">{{cite journal |last1=Tchotet Tchoumi |first1=J. M. |last2=Coetzee |first2=M. P. A. |last3=Rajchenberg |first3=M. |last4=Wingfield |first4=M. J. |last5=Roux |first5=J. |s2cid=49539789 |title=Three ''Ganoderma'' species, including ''Ganoderma dunense'' sp. nov., associated with dying ''Acacia cyclops'' trees in South Africa |journal=Australasian Plant Pathology |date=29 June 2018 |volume=47 |issue=4 |pages=431–447 |doi=10.1007/s13313-018-0575-7 |bibcode=2018AuPP...47..431T |hdl=2263/66186 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> ''A. cyclops'' is problematic in coastal and lowland parts of the Cape Provinces. The species was introduced in the 1830s where it was used as a dune stabiliser and by 1975 it occupied around {{cvt|300000|ha}} of coastal lowlands, and sandy river valleys of inland areas forming dense thickets.<ref name=lucid/>

==Uses==
[[Indigenous Australians]] grind the seeds into a flour to make [[bush bread|damper]], the seeds are a good source of carbohydrates, fats and protein. The seeds pods are also crushed while still green to make an insect repellent and sunscreen that is also used to treat [[eczema]].<ref name="mooro" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Hansen|first1=V.|title=Noongar Bush Medicine Medicinal plants of the south-west of Western Australia|last2=Horsefall|first2=J.|publisher=University of Western Australia|year=2016|isbn=978-1-74258-906-0|location=Crawley, WA|pages=137}}</ref>  The pods can also be used to make a soap solution. The edible gum exuded from the trunk can be used as chewing gum or to make a glue. The wood is used to make a variety of tools and the rotten wood is a good source of [[witchetty grub]]s.<ref name="mooro" />

Red-eyed wattle can also be used to help stabilise coastal sands.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Beer |first=Hildegard |title=Rooikrans |url=https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/Leaflets%20Library/RooikransEng.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210303144516/https://www.arc.agric.za/arc-ppri/Leaflets%20Library/RooikransEng.pdf |archive-date=3 March 2021 |access-date=26 March 2025 |website=Farming in South Africa}}</ref> It was introduced into [[Africa]] for this purpose, but it has spread rapidly and is now a serious pest in southern Africa, where it is known as '''rooikrans''' (in [[Afrikaans]], "red garland"). The introduction of the gall-forming cecidomyiid ''Dasineura dielsi'' as a [[biological control]] has had only limited success in the effective control of the species in these areas.

The green seed pods may be used as a natural soap, by crushing them and using the pods with water to wash with.
